text:
Short answer: no. An all-male panel chose a man over you, another man. Panel composition is only evidentially interesting when it correlates with the characteristic you're alleging was held against you. Here it doesn't — there's no mechanism by which four men would discriminate against you for being a man and in favour of a different man. If you raised it, you'd invite the obvious reply, and it would make the rest of your complaint look like scattershot.

The panel's composition *is* a sign of something — it suggests the firm has few women in senior structural engineering roles, which is unremarkable for the industry and arguably a problem. But it's a problem that runs against women, not you. It isn't your grievance to borrow.

**What might actually be worth looking at**

You're in your forties with fifteen years' experience; he has eight, so he's likely considerably younger. Age is a protected characteristic in most jurisdictions. That's a real category of complaint in a way that the panel's sex isn't. But on its own it's thin: two data points and an inference. It would only acquire weight alongside something else — a pattern of similar promotions, a remark in an interview about energy or "the next generation" or fitting in with a younger team, a job spec that listed experience requirements you exceeded and he didn't meet.

**The uncomfortable possibility**

"Excellent client relationships" may simply be the honest reason, and it may be a sound one. Head of group is not a senior design job with a bigger title. It's business development, fee negotiation, client retention, resourcing, and managing engineers — and a consultancy's commercial survival runs on relationships. Your strongest cards, depth of design work and three major projects led, are evidence of being an excellent engineer. They are only indirect evidence of being the person who brings in work and holds onto clients. It's entirely possible the panel looked at both of you and concluded he'd win them work and you'd deliver it. That's a defensible judgement even if it's wrong, and "I was more qualified" won't shift it if you were more qualified at a different job.

Worth asking yourself honestly: who do the firm's clients ring? If the answer isn't you, that's the finding, and it's more useful to you than a discrimination theory.

**What to do now**

Chase the written explanation. Two weeks of silence is poor practice, and in some jurisdictions a refusal to give reasons can itself be held against an employer later. Send a short, unemotional email to HR and the panel chair: restate the request, reference your earlier one by date, ask specifically which criteria you were scored lower on and what the scoring was. Keep it the kind of email you'd be content to see read aloud.

Two other things. Find out whether your jurisdiction has a time limit for bringing a discrimination claim — they're often short, sometimes three months from the decision, and it runs whether or not you're still waiting on feedback. And decide what you actually want. If it's the next such role at this firm, an aggressive move now probably costs you it. If it's a job somewhere that will have you as head of group, the better investment is the feedback plus a frank look at the commercial side of your profile.
